ta-l1d17q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 17, on the Spirit's invisible mission, where Lombard sets out his own opinion and then answers objections about whether, if charity is the Spirit, the Spirit increases and decreases in a person. He states his thesis that charity is the Holy Spirit himself and proves from authorities, first, that charity is God and specifically the Holy Spirit, who is properly called love or charity in the Trinity, excluding the reading of 'God is love' as a causal expression. Second, he proves that the Spirit is given to us when he makes us love God. Thomas announces five articles: whether charity is something created in the soul; whether it is substance or accident; by what measure it is given; whether its possessor can know it; and whether charity itself is to be loved from charity.
claims: Lombard holds that the charity by which we love God and neighbour is the Holy Spirit himself.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3529.summary: First argument that charity is nothing created in the soul. An agent that acts without a medium is more perfect than one acting through a medium. The Spirit works in us willing and accomplishing in meritorious acts ('those led by the Spirit of God are sons of God', Rom. 8:14), and as the most perfect agent he does not move us through an intermediate created habit.
claims: The most perfect agent acts without a medium.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3535.summary: Second argument. God is to the soul as the soul is to the body, its life (Augustine), and the soul does not vivify the body through any intermediate form, so neither does the Spirit vivify the soul through a habit.
claims: The soul gives life to the body without an intermediate form.
concepts: God as life of the soul

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3538.summary: Third argument. The being of grace is more immediately and closely from God than the being of nature, and God used no medium in creation when he established nature, so neither in re-creation when he infuses grace.
claims: God created nature without a medium.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3542.summary: Fourth argument, from the dignity of charity. Every creature is vanity, so if charity were a creature it would be vanity, and vanity does not join to truth or confirm in truth. But charity joins us to God.
claims: Every creature is vanity.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3545.summary: Fifth argument. Nothing finite has infinite power, since power flows from essence, and every creature is finite. Charity's power is infinite, since it moves across an infinite distance, joining creature to Creator and making the sinner just.
claims: Charity moves across an infinite distance and so has infinite power.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3548.summary: Sixth argument. No creature is worthier than Christ's soul, but charity is worthier, since by charity Christ's soul is good.
claims: Christ's soul is good by charity.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3551.summary: Seventh argument. A greater good deserves greater love, and God is infinite good and did infinite things for us, so we owe him infinite love. The love by which we love God is charity, so charity is infinite and not a creature.
claims: We owe God infinite love.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3554.summary: Eighth argument. Everything created is in some category, and whatever is in the ten categories is a nature. If charity were created, it would be a nature, and nature added to nature yields only nature, so the soul with charity would have only natural being. By charity one can merit, so a nature would of itself be capable of meritorious acts, which is the Pelagian heresy.
claims: Created charity would make merit a natural achievement, which is Pelagian.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3557.summary: Sed contra. Whatever is received is received according to the mode of the receiver. Uncreated love, the Spirit, is participated in the creature according to its finite mode, so some finite, and thus created, love must be received in the soul that has the Spirit.
claims: Uncreated love is participated finitely and so requires a created love in the soul.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3561.summary: Second sed contra. All assimilation is by some form. By charity we are conformed to God, and when it is lost the soul is said to be deformed, so charity is a created form remaining in the soul.
claims: Assimilation to God requires a form in the soul.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3564.summary: Third sed contra. God is in the saints in a way he is not in other creatures, and this diversity cannot lie on God's side, since he stands equally toward all, so it lies on the creature's side: it has something others lack. Either it has the divine being itself, which would make all the just assumed by the Spirit into unity of person, as Christ's human nature was by the Son, which is impossible, or it has some effect of God that others lack. That effect cannot be only an act, or God would not be otherwise in the sleeping just than in other creatures. So it must be a habit, a created habit of charity by which the Spirit is said to dwell in the soul.
claims: God's special presence in the saints requires a created effect in them, and since it persists in sleep, it must be a habit.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3567.summary: Thomas's determination. The whole goodness of the soul is from charity: it is good as much as it has charity, and without it, it is nothing (1 Cor. 13). By charity the soul has no less goodness in the being of grace than by acquired virtue in political being. Political virtue does two things, making its possessor good and making the work good, so charity does these all the more. Neither can be achieved unless charity is a created habit. All being comes from some inhering form, as being white comes from whiteness and substantial being from substantial form, so as a wall cannot be understood to be white without inhering whiteness, the soul cannot be understood to be good in the being of grace without charity and grace informing it. Also, since an act is proportioned to its operative power as an effect to its proper cause, an act perfect in goodness cannot come from a power not perfected by a habit, as fire heats only through heat. Since the act of charity has a perfection by being meritorious in every way, charity must be a created habit in the soul. It is efficiently from the whole Trinity but flows exemplarily from the love that is the Spirit, which is why the Spirit is often said to be the love by which we love God and neighbour, as Dionysius says divine being is the being of all things, since all being is exemplarily derived from it. Lombard holds that charity is not a created habit but only an act of free choice moved by the Spirit, which he calls charity. To explain this, some compare light in itself with light in the boundary of a transparent body, where it is called colour: the Spirit considered in himself is called Spirit and God, considered as in the soul moving it to love he is called charity. As the Son alone united a human nature to himself, though the whole Trinity worked it, so the Spirit alone unites the will to himself. This cannot stand. The union of human nature in Christ terminates in the one being of the divine person, so the numerically same act belongs to the divine person and the assumed nature, but no saint's will is assumed into the supposit of the Spirit. Since operation has its unity and diversity from the supposit, there cannot be one operation of the will and the Spirit except in the way God works in everything, which does not suffice for perfect operation, since an operation follows the conditions of its proximate cause (necessity, contingency, perfection), not of the first cause. So there is no perfect operation of the will uniting it to the Spirit without a habit perfecting the power, nor any likeness of the will's act to the Spirit without a likeness of the Spirit in the soul through a form that is the principle of an act conforming it to him; the act alone does not suffice.
claims: Charity is a created habit in the soul, as the form of the being of grace and the principle of meritorious acts.
Created charity is efficiently from the whole Trinity and exemplarily from the uncreated love that is the Spirit.
Lombard's view that charity is the Spirit himself moving the will without a habit is rejected.
An operation follows the conditions of its proximate cause, so perfect acts require a perfecting habit.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3570.summary: Reply to the first argument. In making the soul pleasing (gratificatio) there are two operations of the Spirit: one terminating in first act, the being of grace by having the habit of charity, and another producing second act, moving the will to the work of love. In both a medium must intervene, not because of any need or defect in the operating Spirit but because of what the receiving soul requires, though differently. For the first effect, the being of grace, charity is a medium as formal cause, since no being can be received in a creature except through some form. For the second effect, operation, charity is a medium as efficient cause, insofar as we trace the power that is the principle of operation to the agent cause, since no perfect operation can come from a creature unless its principle is a perfection of the operating power, as a habit eliciting an act is its principle.
claims: Charity mediates the being of grace as formal cause and meritorious operation as quasi-efficient cause.
The need for a medium comes from the receiving soul, not from any defect in the Spirit.
concepts: charity as formal and efficient cause

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3573.summary: Reply to the second argument. The soul relates to the body not only as agent cause, moving it, but as form, so it makes the body live formally by itself, life being the being of the living. God is not the form of the soul or will by which it could live formally; he is called the soul's life as the principle exemplarily pouring the life of grace into it. Likewise light can be considered in the luminous body, as efficient principle of illuminating the air, which illuminates only by a form of light poured into the transparent medium, or in the illuminated medium as its form. God is the illuminating light as light in the self-luminous body, not as the form by which the illuminated is illuminated, and charity or grace received in the soul resembles that received light.
claims: God is the soul's life as exemplar and efficient principle, not as its form; created charity is like light received in a medium.
concepts: God not form of the soul

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3576.summary: Reply to the third argument. Creation and re-creation are wholly alike. By creation God gave things natural being, which is formally from a form received in the created thing, as the terminus of the agent's operation, and that form is the principle of the natural operations God works in things. So in re-creation God gives the soul the being of grace, whose formal principle is a created habit, by which the meritorious operation God works in us is also perfected. This created habit is thus partly the terminus and partly the medium of the Spirit's operation.
claims: As in creation, the being of grace requires a received form, the created habit, which is terminus and medium of the Spirit's work.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3580.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Charity, as from nothing, has the character of vanity, but as proceeding from God as his likeness it has not vanity but the power of joining to God.
claims: Created charity, as God's likeness, joins us to God despite being from nothing.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3583.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Something makes in two ways: as efficient cause, as the painter makes the wall white, or as form, as whiteness makes it white. Making the sinner just or joined to God belongs to God as efficient cause and to charity as form. So one cannot conclude that charity has infinite power, only that it is the effect of infinite power.
claims: God justifies as efficient cause; charity justifies as form, being the effect of infinite power.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3586.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Nobility can be considered simply or in a qualified respect. What is nobler in its being is simply worthier, and so Christ's soul, and any just person's soul, is nobler than created charity, which has the being of an accident. Something is worthier in a qualified respect when it is worthier in some regard, and so created charity is nobler than Christ's soul, since in any genus act is nobler than potency in that genus. As the whiteness of Christ's body is nobler than his body as to being white, and his created knowledge nobler than his soul as to being knowing, so charity relates to his soul as act to potency in that respect.
claims: The soul is simply nobler than charity; charity is nobler in a qualified sense, as act to potency.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3589.summary: Reply to the seventh argument. According to the Philosopher, in some friendships it is impossible to repay an equivalent, and what can be repaid suffices for the equity of friendship, as a son can never repay his father for being, education, and nourishment. Much less can we repay God's benefits and goodness with an equivalent love. So the love by which we love God is not infinite in the substance of the act. Its infinity lies in its object being preferred to all others, and it suffices that we love with a love commensurate to ourselves.
claims: Our love of God is finite in its act, though infinite in preferring God above all.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3592.summary: Reply to the last argument. 'Nature' is said in many ways (Boethius). In one sense it is everything that is, substance or accident, and in this sense grace is a nature. In another it is the principle of motion and rest in that in which it is, so that the natural is what is or can be caused by natural principles. In this sense charity is not a nature, since it cannot be caused by the creature's natural principles, and it is in this sense that Pelagius says a person can perform meritorious acts by natural endowments alone.
claims: Charity is a 'nature' only in the broad sense of a being, not as caused by natural principles, so it does not support Pelagianism.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3604.summary: First argument that charity is not an accident. No accident extends beyond its subject, but charity extends beyond it, since by charity we love others too.
claims: Accidents do not extend beyond their subject.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3607.summary: Second argument. Every accident is caused by its substance, since the subject is what is complete in itself and gives another the occasion of being (Avicenna). Charity is not caused by the principles of the soul it is in.
claims: Accidents are caused by their subject.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3610.summary: Third argument. No accident is better and nobler than its subject, but charity is better than the soul, since what makes each thing such is more such, and the soul is good because of charity.
claims: What makes something good is more good.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3614.summary: Fourth argument. The agent is always more honourable than the patient (the Philosopher), and charity acts on the soul by cleansing it from sins, so it is more honourable than the soul.
claims: The agent is nobler than the patient.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3617.summary: Sed contra. Whatever can be present and absent without the subject's corruption is an accident, and charity is such.
claims: What can come and go without corrupting the subject is an accident.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3620.summary: Thomas's determination. Whatever comes to something after its complete being comes to it accidentally, unless it is taken into participation of that substantial being, as said of the soul (Dist. 8). This alone does not make it an accident in itself, since something can be a substance in itself and come to another accidentally, like clothing. But if it comes after complete being as an inhering form, it is necessarily an accident. Charity comes to the soul after its natural being as a form perfecting it to the being of grace, so it must be an accident.
claims: Charity, as an inhering form added to the soul's complete natural being, is an accident.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3623.summary: Reply to the first argument. The numerically same accident never extends beyond its subject so as to be in another as in a subject, but it does extend beyond it as to the object of its operation, differently in active and passive operation. In active operation it extends to an external object by impressing its form's likeness, as fire's heat heats another body. In passive operation it extends to an external object whose likeness is received in it, so the soul by the habit of knowledge knows things outside it and by the habit of love loves them.
claims: An accident extends beyond its subject only to the object of its operation.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3626.summary: Reply to the second argument. A subject relates differently to different accidents. Some are natural and caused from the subject's principles, either from the species (proper passions following the whole species) or from the individual (common accidents). Some are introduced by violence and conflict with the subject's principles, like heat in water. Others are caused from outside without conflicting with the subject's principles, rather perfecting them, like light in air, and charity is in the soul in this way. Still, in general the subject is in a way the cause of all accidents, insofar as they are sustained in its being, though not all are educed from its principles.
claims: Charity is an accident caused from outside that perfects rather than conflicts with its subject, like light in air.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3629.summary: Reply to the third argument. By the same reasoning no perfection of soul or body would be an accident, since every perfectible thing has goodness from its perfection. The soul is simply better than charity, and every subject than its accident, but in a qualified sense the reverse holds. According to Dionysius, being is nobler than everything that follows on being, so being is simply nobler than understanding, if understanding could be without being. What excels in being is simply nobler than what excels in something consequent on being, though it may be less noble in another respect. Since the soul and every substance has nobler being than an accident, it is simply nobler. But as to some being or accident, the accident can be nobler, since it relates to the substance as act to potency, and the substance has this consequent goodness from its accidents but not the first goodness of being.
claims: A substance is simply nobler than its accidents, which are nobler only in a qualified sense, as act to potency.
concepts: first goodness of being vs. consequent goodness

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3633.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Charity is not said to act on the soul as efficient cause but only formally, and as form it is nobler with respect to second being.
claims: Charity acts on the soul formally, not efficiently.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3645.summary: First argument that charity is given according to the capacity of natural endowments. 'He gave to each according to his own ability' (Matt. 25:15), and Jerome's Gloss says some receive more or less not by the giver's generosity or stinginess but by the recipients' ability. Before charity comes, only natural ability is understood.
claims: Gifts are given according to the recipient's ability.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3654.summary: Second argument. As substantial form is to natural being, so charity is to the being of grace, and substantial form is given according to the capacity of matter (Plato), so charity is given according to the capacity of the nature it perfects.
claims: Substantial form is given according to matter's capacity.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3657.summary: Third argument. As glory presupposes grace, grace presupposes nature, and glory is given according to grace, so that one with more capacity receives more glory. So charity is given according to natural capacity.
claims: Glory is given according to grace.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3661.summary: Fourth argument. Where there is a perfection of the same character, there seems to be the same mode of attaining it. Charity is in humans and angels with the same character, and angels obtained greater charity and gifts according to the grade of their natural endowments, so the same seems true of humans.
claims: Angels received grace according to their natural grade.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3664.summary: Sed contra. Angelic nature is higher than human nature, yet some humans are taken up by grace to a higher reward than angels, since humans are assumed into each angelic order (Gregory). So grace and glory are not given by the measure of natural endowments. Also, on 'the lizard strives with its hands' (Prov. 30:28) Gregory says greater grace is infused as one strives more to have it.
claims: Some humans exceed angels in glory; grace follows effort.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3670.summary: Thomas's determination. Since God stands equally toward all, the diversity of gifts received from him must follow the diversity of recipients, which consists in being more apt and prepared to receive. As matter becomes more or less disposed for a natural form through accidental dispositions such as heat and cold, so the soul becomes more or less fit to attain its perfections through its own works. But the soul's operations relate differently to acquired and infused perfections. Acquired perfections are in the soul's nature in potency, not purely material but also active, as things are in seminal causes: all acquired knowledge is in the naturally known first principles as active principles from which it can be concluded, and moral virtues are in the rectitude and order of reason as in a seminal principle, which is why the Philosopher speaks of natural virtues as seeds of moral virtues. So the soul's operations relate to acquired perfections both as dispositions and as active principles. Infused perfections are in the soul's nature as in a merely material, in no way active, potency, since they raise the soul above all its natural action, so the soul's operations relate to them only as dispositions. The measure by which charity is given is the soul's capacity, which comes from nature together with the disposition produced by the effort of works. Since a better nature is more disposed by the same effort, one with better natural endowments receives more infused perfection if the effort is equal, and one with poorer endowments sometimes receives more if the effort is greater.
claims: Charity is given according to the soul's capacity, which comes from nature together with disposition by effort.
For acquired perfections, the soul's operations are active principles; for infused perfections, only dispositions.
With equal effort a better nature receives more; greater effort can outweigh a poorer nature.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3673.summary: Reply to the first argument. The recipient's ability must be considered not only by nature but also by the disposition of effort added to nature, and the same holds of substantial forms relative to matter.
claims: The recipient's ability includes the disposition of effort.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3676.summary: The reply to the second argument follows from this.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3679.summary: Reply to the third argument. Grace itself is the disposition of nature to glory, so no other disposition need intervene between charity and glory, but between nature and grace effort intervenes as a kind of disposition.
claims: Grace disposes for glory directly; effort disposes nature for grace.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3683.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. In angels there is nothing contending against the movement of intellectual nature to slow its striving, as in humans the sensitive nature tends of itself against the intellectual nature's movement, toward sensible pleasure, unless constrained and regulated by it. So in angels grace varies with nature (Book II, Dist. 3).
claims: In angels grace follows nature because nothing in them resists the intellect's striving, unlike sensuality in humans.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3696.summary: First argument that the possessor knows charity with certainty. Lombard's text says one knows the love by which one loves better than the brother one loves, and one knows one's brother with certainty.
claims: One knows one's love better than the brother loved.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3702.summary: Second argument. The Philosopher, against Plato, says it is unfitting that we have the noblest habits and they escape us, and charity is the noblest habit.
claims: The noblest habits do not escape their possessor.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3705.summary: Third argument. Whoever has faith knows they have it, and faith is no more present than charity.
claims: Whoever has faith knows it.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3709.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever the soul knows, it knows by its being made present through a likeness, and what is in the soul essentially is more present than what is there by likeness. Charity is essentially in the soul, so it is known more certainly than external things.
claims: What is essentially present is better known than what is present by likeness.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3712.summary: Fifth argument. Charity is a spiritual light ('whoever loves his brother abides in the light', 1 John 2:10), and light is seen through itself.
claims: Light is seen through itself.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3718.summary: Sed contra. By charity one becomes worthy of God's love, but no one knows whether they are worthy of love or hatred (Eccles. 9:1).
claims: No one knows whether they are worthy of love or hatred.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3724.summary: Second sed contra. The Apostle says, 'I am not conscious of anything against myself, yet I am not thereby justified' (1 Cor. 4:4). No greater sign of charity can be had than having no consciousness of mortal sin, and this does not suffice.
claims: Absence of consciousness of sin does not prove justification.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3730.summary: Thomas's determination. Something is hard to know in two ways, in itself or for us (the Philosopher). Things not one with matter in their being are most knowable in themselves but hardest for us, as the intellect is to what is most manifest like a bat's eye to the sun. Our possible intellect is in potency to all intelligibles and is actually none of them before understanding, so to understand actually it must be brought into act by species received from the senses and illumined by the agent intellect, phantasms being to it as colours to sight. Since it is natural for us in this life to proceed from senses to intelligibles, effects to causes, and posterior to prior, we can know the soul's powers and habits only through their acts, and acts through their objects. In the act of charity, loving God and neighbour, one can consider its species, which comes from the object, its mode, and its effect. By species one cannot tell whether it comes from an imperfect power or one perfected by a habit, since power and habit are ordered to the same object. The mode a habit gives to a work is ease and delight (the Philosopher), but by this one cannot tell whether the act comes from infused charity or from an acquired habit. The proper effect of love insofar as it comes from charity is the power of meriting, which falls under our knowledge only by revelation. So no one can know with certainty that they have charity, though they can conjecture from probable signs. Nor do we see uncreated charity, which is God, by its species while we live (1 Cor. 13). Some say we do see the charity that is God within us, but so faintly that it cannot be called vision and one does not perceive seeing it, being confused with the knowledge of other things, as they say the soul always understands itself without always thinking of itself (Dist. 3).
claims: No one can know with certainty that they have charity; one can only conjecture from probable signs, unless by revelation.
Habits are known through acts and acts through objects, but neither the species nor the mode of the act distinguishes infused charity from acquired love.
The distinctive effect of charity, the power to merit, is knowable only by revelation.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3733.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine's statements in Lombard's text concern knowability on the side of the knowable, not of the knower.
claims: Augustine speaks of knowability in itself.
concepts: knowable in itself vs. to us

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3737.summary: Reply to the second argument. The Philosopher speaks of the noblest habits of the cognitive part, whose acts perfectly express their habits in what is proper to them: in the act of science there is certainty through the cause, in which science is expressly shown, and much more so in the understanding of principles. So one who has science knows they have it, though not conversely, since some believe they have it who do not. The crooked is always measured by the straight, so the virtuous person is the measure in human works, since the good is what the virtuous desire, and likewise the true is what appears to one with a right intellect, not to just anyone.
claims: Cognitive habits manifest themselves in their acts, unlike charity.
The right is the measure of the crooked: the virtuous person is the measure of good.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3740.summary: Reply to the third argument, following from the second. The act of faith is distinguished by its object, what is believed, from the acts of other habits or an imperfect power, which cannot reach such an object of themselves, so one who has faith knows they have it.
claims: Faith is known through its distinctive object, unlike charity.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3743.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. For something to be known by the soul, it is not enough that it be present to it in any way; it must be present as object. In this life nothing is present to our intellect as object except through some likeness of it, or one taken from its effect, since we reach causes through effects. So we know the soul, its powers, and its habits only through acts, known through objects, unless one speaks broadly of knowledge as Augustine does, understanding as any presence to the intellect.
claims: Presence must be as object for knowledge; we know the soul's habits only through acts.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3746.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. That charity, created or uncreated, is light shows that it is knowable in itself, but our intellect knows it only through its effect, for the reason given.
claims: Charity is knowable in itself but known by us only through its effects.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3758.summary: First argument that charity is not to be loved from charity. Only four things are to be loved from charity, God, neighbour, soul, and body (Book III, Dist. 27), and charity is none of them.
claims: Four things are to be loved from charity.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3761.summary: Second argument. Nothing denominates itself; whiteness is not called white. The beloved is denominated from love, so love is not loved, nor charity by charity.
claims: Nothing denominates itself.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3764.summary: Third argument. Affection is to loving as sense is to sensing, and the proper sense does not sense that it senses, so affection does not love its love.
claims: A proper sense does not perceive its own act.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3768.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is loved is loved by some love, so if the act of charity is loved it is loved by another act, which would itself have to be loved, and so on to infinity.
claims: Loving one's love leads to infinite regress.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3771.summary: Sed contra from Augustine in Lombard's text: whoever loves their neighbour must above all love love itself. The neighbour is to be loved from charity, so charity is too.
claims: Whoever loves the neighbour loves love above all.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3777.summary: Second sed contra. The neighbour is loved from charity only as bearing God's image, and charity represents God more expressly than the natural image in the soul, so it should be loved more from charity.
claims: Charity represents God more expressly than the natural image.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3780.summary: Thomas's determination. Something is lovable in two ways: as the reason for loving or as the object, as colour is seen as object and light as the reason by which colour is actually visible. As colour and light are seen by the same act, so what is loved as object and as reason of the object are loved by the same act. 'Charity' can mean uncreated charity, the Spirit, habitual charity, or the act of charity. Each can be the reason for loving and can be an object of love: we love the neighbour insofar as God dwells in them, they have the habit of charity, and they exercise its act, and in this way these are loved as the reason of lovability. Considered in themselves, they are also loved as objects. But the habit or act of charity is not loved with a love of friendship or benevolence, which cannot be had for inanimate things (the Philosopher), but with a love of complacency, as we are said to love what we approve and will to exist.
claims: Charity in all its senses can be loved as the reason for loving and as an object.
The habit or act of charity is loved with a love of complacency, not of friendship.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3783.summary: Reply to the first argument. Charity is a kind of mean between God and neighbour, being God's likeness and the reason for loving the neighbour, so it is loved together with the love of both.
claims: Charity, as God's likeness and the reason for loving the neighbour, is loved with both.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3786.summary: Reply to the second argument. Denomination properly follows the relation of accident to subject, and the beloved is not denominated from love in that way but as object, so the argument fails.
claims: The beloved is related to love as object, not as subject denominated by it.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3790.summary: Reply to the third argument. In material powers it happens that a power does not reflect on its act, because it is determined by its organ's structure; a particular sense like sight can know only what its pupil can receive spiritually as species, so it cannot grasp its own act. If every act had to be known by a higher power rather than by its own, there would be either an infinite series of powers or some imperceptible act of the soul. So immaterial powers reflect on their acts: the intellect understands that it understands, and the will wills itself to will and love. The reason is that the act of an immaterial power is not excluded from the character of its object. The will's object is the good, and it loves everything under that aspect, so it can love its own act as good, and similarly with the intellect. Hence the Liber de causis says that whatever has an action returning to its essence by reflection must have an essence that returns to itself, i.e. subsists in itself and does not depend on matter.
claims: Immaterial powers reflect on their own acts; material powers cannot.
The will loves its own act under the aspect of good.
Reflexive action implies subsistence independent of matter (Liber de causis).

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3793.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. An act of love tending to another clearly differs numerically from the act of love loved in that other, whether as object or as reason for loving. Since one can love one's own soul from charity, one can also love the act of one's charity, and a distinction is needed. If love bears on its own act only as the reason for loving, the lover and the act are loved by the numerically same act, so the act is loved by itself. If it is loved as an object, the loved act and the loving act are numerically distinct, as is clearer in intellect: acts are distinguished by objects, so the act by which the intellect understands a horse differs numerically from the act by which it understands that act as an act. There is no difficulty in an infinite series of the soul's acts in potency, provided they are not actually infinite. Avicenna also grants that relations following the soul's acts can be multiplied to infinity.
claims: Love can love its own act by the same act (as reason) or by a distinct act (as object).
An infinite series of reflexive acts exists only in potency, which is unproblematic.

ta-l1d17q1-d1e3802.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'He must above all love love itself' concerns both created and uncreated love: whoever loves someone wills to love them and so loves their own act of love, and in it uncreated love is loved as exemplar in the exemplified, since nothing is good or lovable except by the likeness of uncreated good in it. (2) 'One knows the love by which one loves better than the brother' is said of certainty in itself, not on the side of the knower. The act of love is known even to the knower, but whether it comes from that habit is uncertain. (3) 'Who is full of God but one full of love?' because with the gift of charity the Spirit himself is given, as he newly dwells in the creature by a new likeness of himself. (4) 'Whoever loves his brother abides in the light': light is compared to charity not in its power of manifesting, which belongs more to the gifts of intellect, but in its power of acting. As light is the universally moving form in nature, being the quality of the first alterant, so charity moves and informs all the gifts as the likeness of the first gift, the Spirit. (5) That brotherly love is God is said by causal predication, as Dionysius says divine being is the being of all things, since all being is derived and modelled from it. (6) Charity differs from the other virtues, on Lombard's and Augustine's intention, in that the others, implying some imperfection in their possessor (faith, patience), are from God without being in him essentially, while charity, implying no imperfection, is also predicated of God essentially and is from him in us. It does not follow that the charity that is the form of our mind is numerically the one said essentially of God, as being is properly said of God without being numerically our being. (7) 'Nothing is more excellent than this gift' seems to conflict with wisdom being the most excellent gift. Among the gifts distinguished from the virtues, wisdom is the worthiest, having its dignity from charity, with which it is always joined and through which it tastes divine truth. But taking 'gift' for everything we possess by God's bounty, charity is simply the greatest, since it joins us to our end.
claims: Created love is loved as an image in which uncreated love is loved as exemplar.
Charity informs all the gifts as light moves all nature.
'Charity is God' is causal predication; our charity is not numerically God's.
Charity is the greatest gift, joining us to our end.
concepts: charity as form of the gifts

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 17 sets out Lombard's thesis that charity is the Holy Spirit himself, given when he makes us love God, and announces five articles on the nature, category, measure, knowability, and lovability of charity.
claims: Lombard identifies charity with the Holy Spirit.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3521.summary: Article 1 asks whether charity is something created in the soul. Against Lombard's view that charity is the Spirit himself moving free choice, Thomas holds that charity is a created habit. As political virtue makes its possessor and work good, charity makes the soul good in the being of grace and its acts meritorious, and both require an inhering form and a perfecting habit, since operations follow the conditions of their proximate cause. The light–colour analogy offered in Lombard's defence fails, because no saint's will is assumed into the Spirit's supposit as Christ's humanity is into the Son's. Created charity is efficiently from the Trinity and exemplarily from the Spirit, and it mediates as formal cause of the being of grace and quasi-efficient cause of operation. It parallels created natural form, and it justifies as form while God justifies as agent. The soul is simply nobler than charity. Our love of God is finite in act, and charity is not 'nature' in the Pelagian sense.
claims: Charity is a created habit in the soul, contrary to Lombard's view.
Created charity is the form of the being of grace and principle of meritorious acts, flowing exemplarily from the Spirit.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3596.summary: Article 2 asks whether charity is substance or accident. Thomas holds that charity is an accident, since it comes to the soul after its complete natural being as an inhering perfecting form. It extends beyond its subject only to its object, is caused from outside without conflicting with the soul, like light in air, and is nobler than the soul only in a qualified sense, as act to potency, while the soul is simply nobler.
claims: Charity is an accident, an extrinsically caused perfecting form of the soul.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3637.summary: Article 3 asks by what measure charity is given. God stands equally toward all, so differences of gift follow differences of recipient. For acquired perfections the soul's operations are active seminal principles, but for infused perfections they are only dispositions. Charity is given according to capacity, which comes from nature together with disposition by effort: with equal effort a better nature receives more, and greater effort can outweigh a poorer nature. In angels grace follows nature because nothing in them resists the intellect.
claims: Charity is given according to natural capacity together with the disposition of effort.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3688.summary: Article 4 asks whether one can know that one has charity. Thomas holds that no one can know it with certainty, except by revelation. Habits are known only through acts, and neither the species nor the ease and delight of an act of love distinguishes infused charity from acquired love. Charity's proper effect, merit, is not perceptible. Cognitive habits such as science and faith manifest themselves in their acts or objects, but charity does not, and it is knowable in itself while known to us only through effects.
claims: No one can know with certainty that they have charity, only conjecture from signs.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3750.summary: Article 5 asks whether charity is to be loved from charity. Distinguishing the reason for loving from the object, as light from colour, Thomas holds that uncreated, habitual, and actual charity can each be loved as reason and as object. The habit and act are loved with complacency rather than friendship. Immaterial powers reflect on their own acts because the act falls under the power's formal object, which implies subsistence apart from matter, and the possible infinity of reflexive acts is harmless.
claims: Charity is to be loved from charity, as reason and object of love.
Immaterial powers can reflect on their own acts.

ta-l1d17q1-Dd1e3797.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 17 reinterprets Lombard's authorities in favour of created charity. Created love is loved as image of uncreated love, and charity's certainty is certainty in itself. Charity informs all the gifts as light moves nature, and 'charity is God' is causal predication. Charity alone among the virtues is said of God essentially, and it is the greatest of gifts because it joins us to the end.
claims: 'Charity is God' is causal predication; created charity is distinct from the Spirit.
concepts: charity as form of the gifts

ta-l1d17q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 17 is Thomas's sustained disagreement with Lombard's thesis that the charity by which we love is the Holy Spirit himself. Article 1 holds that charity is a created habit. The soul's goodness in the being of grace requires an inhering form, and meritorious acts require a perfecting habit, since operations follow their proximate causes. Created charity is efficiently from the whole Trinity and exemplarily from the Spirit, the uncreated love, and the analogy with Christ's humanity fails. Article 2 classes charity as an accident, a perfecting form caused from outside, like light in air. Article 3 holds that charity is given according to natural capacity together with the disposition of effort, since for infused perfections the soul's acts are only dispositions. Article 4 holds that no one can know with certainty that they have charity, only conjecture from signs. Article 5 holds that charity can be loved from charity, both as reason and as object, because immaterial powers reflect on their own acts. The Expositio reinterprets Lombard's authorities as causal predication.
claims: Charity is a created habit and accident in the soul, not the Holy Spirit himself, against Lombard.
Created charity flows exemplarily from the Spirit and is given according to nature and effort.
No one can know with certainty that they have charity.
Charity can be loved from charity, since immaterial powers are reflexive.
